=={{header|Cxc}}==

Conway's Game of Life models its state as what it actually is: a <em>set of live cells</em>. The <code>alive_cells</code> field is a sparse <code>Set of Cell</code>, not a dense bit grid — a blinker is three Cells, not twenty-five Bools. Grid holds the rule (<code>alive</code>, <code>neighbors</code>, <code>next_cell</code>), the double buffer (<code>alive_cells</code> + <code>staging_next</code>), and the walk. View is a separate atom that owns <code>Console</code> and carries one message, <code>show(board: Grid!)</code>. <code>Cursor(gen, x, y)</code> names the three coordinates that travel together. Grid self-drives through <code>tick(c: Cursor!)</code>, emits <code>:> died</code> on the generation-cap arm, and lets <code>main</code> shrink to a four-line kickoff that waits on <code>g.died</code>. Three generations of a blinker (horizontal → vertical → horizontal) print under this driver.

<syntaxhighlight lang="text">
def Cell:
    x: Int!
    y: Int!

def Cursor:
    gen: Int!
    x:   Int!
    y:   Int!

def View:
    use console: Console

    -> running

    running <: show(board: Grid!) -> running
        range(board.height).for_each(y => console.write(board.row_at(y)))
        console.write("")

def Grid(width: Int!, height: Int!, gens: Int!, view: View!):
    alive_cells: Set of Cell = [Cell(1, 2), Cell(2, 2), Cell(3, 2)]
    staging_next: Set of Cell = []

    offsets: List of Cell = [Cell(-1, -1), Cell(0, -1), Cell(1, -1),
                             Cell(-1,  0),              Cell(1,  0),
                             Cell(-1,  1), Cell(0,  1), Cell(1,  1)]

    alive(x: Int!, y: Int!) :- Bool!
        self.alive_cells.contains(Cell(x, y))

    neighbors(x: Int!, y: Int!) :- Int!
        self.offsets.map(o => self.alive(x + o.x, y + o.y).to_int()).sum()

    next_cell(x: Int!, y: Int!) :- Bool!
        alias n :- self.neighbors(x, y)
        n == 3 or (self.alive(x, y) and n == 2)

    row_at(y: Int!) :- String!
        range(self.width).map(x => ||: self.alive(x, y) : "#" |?: ".").join("")

    done(c: Cursor!) :- Bool!
        c.gen >= self.gens

    row_done(c: Cursor!) :- Bool!
        c.y >= self.height

    col_done(c: Cursor!) :- Bool!
        c.x >= self.width

    -> running
        self :> render
        self :> tick(Cursor(0, 0, 0))

    running <: render -> running
        |> self.view.show(self)

    running <: step_cell(c: Cursor!):
        |:  self.next_cell(c.x, c.y) -> running
            staging_next => self.staging_next.insert(Cell(c.x, c.y))
        |?: -> running

    running <: tick(c: Cursor!):
        |:  self.done(c) -> end
            :> died
        |:  self.row_done(c) -> running
            alive_cells  => self.staging_next
            staging_next => self.staging_next.empty()
            self :> render
            self :> tick(Cursor(c.gen + 1, 0, 0))
        |:  self.col_done(c) -> running
            self :> tick(Cursor(c.gen, 0, c.y + 1))
        |?: -> running
            self :> step_cell(c)
            self :> tick(Cursor(c.gen, c.x + 1, c.y))

def main:
    v: View = View()
    g: Grid = Grid(5, 5, 2, v)
    -> running
    running <: g.died -> end
</syntaxhighlight>

A few notes for readers coming from imperative Life implementations:

* <code>alive_cells: Set of Cell</code> is the state. The initial blinker is three Cells; no padding zeros, no grid-size encoding leak. The record <code>Cell</code> hashes and compares by value — two <code>Cell(2, 2)</code> literals constructed at different call sites are set-equal, which is what membership needs. Positional ctor args (<code>Cell(2, 2)</code> rather than <code>Cell(x: 2, y: 2)</code>) carry the geometry on the line; the field names add visual noise when the two values already read as a point.
* <code>offsets: List of Cell</code> is the eight-neighbor stencil as literal geometry. Life's rule talks about the eight surrounding cells, so the list writes those eight cells out. Deriving the stencil from a 3×3 Cartesian product minus the center is possible but less clear than reading off the geometry directly; the literal is the semantic shape.
* <code>width</code>, <code>height</code>, and <code>gens</code> are ctor params on Grid, so <code>main</code> constructs the grid with <code>Grid(5, 5, 2, v)</code> and the same Grid class runs any grid size or generation cap. Life's rule has no bounds; the set lives on <code>ℤ × ℤ</code>. These parameters bound only the walk and the view.
* <code>alive(x, y)</code> is set membership in one line — no bounds check, no array index. Out-of-range coordinates are just coordinates not in the set.
* <code>neighbors(x, y)</code> maps the stencil over <code>self.alive</code>, converts each <code>Bool</code> to <code>Int</code>, and sums. One pipeline, no hand-written eight-term expression.
* <code>next_cell</code> states the Life rule as its algebra: a cell is alive next tick iff <code>n == 3</code> or (<code>a</code> and <code>n == 2</code>).
* <code>row_at(y)</code> uses <code>range(n)</code> — a built-in that produces <code>List of Int</code> covering <code>[0, n)</code> — then <code>.map</code> renders each column and <code>.join</code> concatenates. Five aliases become one pipeline.
* <code>Cursor(gen, x, y)</code> names the three coordinates that travel together across every <code>tick</code> arm. Three Ints passed positionally through tick's signature would be a data clump; the record names the shape once and lets predicates like <code>done(c)</code>, <code>row_done(c)</code>, <code>col_done(c)</code> dispatch on it.
* Grid's end-of-generation arm reads cleanly as the Life rule algebra: <code>|: self.done(c) -> end</code> terminates on the generation cap, <code>|: self.row_done(c) -> running</code> swaps the double buffer and renders, <code>|: self.col_done(c) -> running</code> advances to the next row, and <code>|?: -> running</code> steps the current cell. The named predicates replace guard arithmetic (<code>c.gen >= self.gens</code> etc.) with intent.
* Each generation advances Grid through two internal messages: <code>step_cell(c)</code> inserts into <code>staging_next</code> when the rule fires, and the row-overflow arm of <code>tick</code> flips the double buffer (<code>alive_cells ← staging_next</code>) and clears the back buffer (<code>staging_next ← .empty()</code>) in one transition. Two stagings on one arm read from the same pre-transition snapshot, so the clear sees the full back buffer before the swap takes effect. The field name <code>staging_next</code> signals operational state, not domain state.
* <code>render</code> enqueues a <code>self :> render</code> self-send rather than reading <code>self.row_at(y)</code> inline. The reason: the arm-body-field-snapshot rule reads every field through a pre-entry snapshot, so a sequence like <code>alive_cells => self.staging_next</code> followed by a direct <code>self.row_at(y)</code> call in the same arm would print the pre-commit state. Splitting render into its own self-sent message re-enters the queue, refreshing the snapshot, so the printed frame is the committed one.
* View is a separate atom. Grid holds a <code>view: View!</code> reference and dispatches with <code>|> self.view.show(self)</code>. Grid passes <code>self</code> so View can walk <code>board.height</code> and <code>board.row_at(y)</code> without carrying its own copy of grid state. The split lets rendering change (colour, Unicode glyphs, a different output sink) without touching Grid's rule or buffer surface.
* <code>main</code> constructs View first, then Grid with the View reference, kicks off, and subscribes to <code>g.died</code> for termination. <code>:> died</code> on Grid's generation-cap arm emits the lifecycle event that <code>main</code>'s <code>running <: g.died -> end</code> handler fires on.
* <code>||:</code> marks an expression-position multi-arm dispatch: the first arm whose guard holds yields its body value. The closing <code>|?:</code> arm covers the no-match case. Together they replace <code>if</code>/<code>else if</code>/<code>else</code>; cxc has no <code>if</code> expression at v1.0.
* <code>|&gt;</code> is a synchronous processing barrier — <code>self.view.show(self)</code> completes before <code>render</code>'s next statement runs. <code>:&gt;</code> (used for <code>self :&gt; tick</code> and <code>self :&gt; render</code>) is async enqueue on the atom's own queue — essential because <code>|&gt;</code> self-sends would deadlock the serial queue (spec §1.11).
* Observation bodies treat each indented line as a separate statement. An intermediate <code>alias</code> breaks a long pipeline across two lines when the full chain would exceed line-width; the alias is pure sugar and has no runtime cost.
